newsitem.title: DUBAI: Bahrain unrest flares anew after lull.
newsitem.headline: Bahrain unrest flares anew after lull.

text.p: After a lull of several months, sporadic civil unrest that has gripped the Gulf Arab state of Bahrain for more than two years has flared anew with a spate of arson attacks on homes and small businesses.
Deaths and injuries have been caused by fires described by a government official as "continued acts of terrorism".

Impoverished Shi'ite Moslem villages in the Gulf's smallest and least wealthy oil-producing country are once again the scene of protests and agitation. Riot police patrol in jeeps by day and by night, when many of the villages are blacked out.
There has been no sign of concern among large international firms in Bahrain, which is the Gulf's main banking and financial centre and is connected to Saudi Arabia by a 25 km causeway.
"Those of us living in dodgy areas hear the odd bomb at night," one expatriate businessman said. "But nothing close."
A car which exploded in the heart of the capital Manama last week caused no casualties, a government official said, but destroyed the vehicle and badly damaged another parked nearby.
"It's a reaction to a massive government crackdown on thousands of Shi'ite Moslems," another foreign resident said.
Shi'ites comprise two-thirds of the population of Bahrain, which has been ruled for two centuries by the Khalifa family who are members of the rival Sunni branch of Islam.

"Some people say it's a message to the government that despite the crackdown on activists people have not backed down from their demands for political and economic reforms," the resident said by telephone.
Among those demands are more job opportunities for Shi'ites.

Asians, who some Bahrainis believe hold jobs which they could do, offer an easy target and have been among the victims. Four Indians died last week from smoke inhalation when fire gutted a shop. Officials called it a premeditated attack.
Seven Bangladeshis died in March 1996 when suspected arsonists set a restaurant ablaze.
More than 30 people have been killed since the unrest began in December 1994, some in clashes with security forces.
International human rights organisations and the exiled opposition accuse security forces, which employ foreigners mainly from the Indian subcontinent, of torturing detainees.
Hundreds have been arrested in connection with the unrest, which reached a peak with bombings at luxury hotels last year. A special state security court has jailed more than 220 people.
Seven Shi'ites were jailed for up to five-and-a-half years on Wednesday for arson offences.
The London-based Bahrain Islamic Freedom Movement said on Wednesday 31 people from various areas had been detained in the previous seven days including a boy aged 11 and a youth aged 16.
Six Shi'ites convicted of possessing unlawful leaflets were fined 200 dinars ($530) but set free because they had already spent 14 months in jail.
Graffiti, systematically obscured by security forces as soon as they are discovered, demand the restoration of the island's parliament, dissolved by the government in 1975.
"Is the parliament a crime?", asks one slogan scrawled on village walls. Another says "The parliament is the solution".
